metric.installation_distribution_experie.limitations: Score reflects a lack of a single canonical package manager (fragmentation across vcpkg/Conan/CPM/Hunter/Bazel) offsetting otherwise excellent native availability of compilers via OS package managers and official vendor installers.
raw_evidence: GCC and Clang have official versioned stable releases (GCC 16.2 / Aug 2026, Clang/LLVM 23.1.0 / Aug 2026) distributed via virtually all Linux package repositories, Homebrew, and Xcode command-line tools.
MSVC ships through the official Visual Studio installer/Build Tools, now on a monthly Visual Studio release cadence with a decoupled compiler lifecycle introduced for Visual Studio 2026.

Two mature, competing cross-platform C/C++ package managers dominate: vcpkg (Microsoft) and Conan (JFrog), both integrating with CMake, but C++ still lacks a single official/standard package manager, and additional competing tools (CPM, Hunter, Buckaroo, Bazel modules) fragment the dependency-distribution experience.

Multiple independent, mature compiler implementations are available and commonly interchangeable (GCC, Clang, MSVC, plus vendor compilers such as Intel C++ Compiler, IBM XL C++, EDG), giving strong redundancy of installable toolchains.

rubric.criterion: Native OS package-manager availability for the compiler/toolchain (apt/dnf/pacman/brew/choco/winget)
Official first-party installer quality across Windows/macOS/Linux
Maturity of a cross-platform dependency/library package manager
Availability of multiple redundant, well-supported toolchain choices (reduces lock-in/failure risk)
Documentation/consistency of setup instructions across platforms

metric.installation_distribution_experie.selection_rule: Toolchains sampled: GCC and Clang (dominant open compilers, ubiquitous in Linux distro repos and macOS/Xcode), MSVC (dominant Windows-first-party compiler). Package managers sampled: vcpkg (Microsoft, official) and Conan (JFrog) as the two managers explicitly identified as the dominant/mature pair in independent overviews.

metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.limitations: C++ has no single unified toolchain vendor, so stability evidence is aggregated across GCC/Clang/MSVC and the ISO standard; ABI stability is a documented Microsoft-specific commitment rather than a universal cross-vendor ISO guarantee, which slightly discounts the compatibility-guarantees and stability-commitments sub-scores.
metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.note_on_language_age: Language age / first-release date is recorded as contextual metadata only per the frozen ecosystem rubric and is not itself scored; only currently observable release/compatibility evidence is scored.
raw_evidence: The ISO C++ standard has followed a strict, documented three-year release cadence since C++11 (2011): C++11, C++14, C++17, C++20, C++23, with C++26 in progress and C++29 already the next planned standard.
C++23 (ISO/IEC 14882:2024) is the current published stable standard, formally finalized by the WG21 committee and published by ISO with a defined administrative process.
WG21 uses a 'train model' where each standard version has a name matching its planned release year, and the committee has hit its planned release year for every cycle so far.
GCC and Clang each ship predictable, versioned stable releases (GCC roughly annual, Clang roughly every ~6 months), both tracked against the ISO C++ standard's timeline.

Microsoft introduced an explicit new MSVC support lifecycle for Visual Studio 2026, designating MSVC 14.50 as a long-term-support (LTS) release, decoupled from the now-monthly Visual Studio IDE cadence, specifically to give predictable long-term stability for build tools.

Microsoft documents an explicit, long-standing ABI stability guarantee: MSVC toolsets from Visual Studio 2015 through 2026 all share major version 14, and Microsoft states that C++ itself lacks a stable ABI but Visual Studio maintains a stable C++ ABI across all of these minor versions, allowing object files, static/dynamic libraries and redistributables built with older toolsets to be linked/used with newer ones.

Prior to Visual Studio 2015, MSVC did not guarantee binary compatibility across major versions; this was a deliberate, documented policy change toward long-term compatibility that has held for over a decade of releases (2015 through 2026).

rubric.criterion: Release reproducibility (deterministic, versioned official release artifacts)
Compatibility guarantees (source and/or ABI stability across versions)
Regularity/predictability of maintenance and release cadence
Documented, frozen stability commitments (formal standardization process, backward-compatibility policy)
